title: Linked lists: node invariants and ownership
lead: Build a small singly linked list using unique_ptr and justify each ownership transfer.
why: A list is useful for understanding linked storage but is not universally fast. Comparing it with vector requires considering lookup, allocation, and the actual operation.
objectives: Explain: A node and the head
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not lose the tail when removing the head. Do not generalize O(1) link changes to position lookup.
prerequisites: Modules 1–2: expressions, comparisons, types, references, and checked cin.
Follow the prerequisite links: cpp.lifetime-ownership, cpp.structures, cpp.testing-diagnostics. New constructs are introduced before the assignment.

concepts.definition: a value together with a link to the next structural element.
the owner of the first node or an empty list.
an owning successor link in this model.
inserting a new node before the former head.
a non-owning address used for a short traversal.
destroying nodes successively without a deep call chain.

sections.title: A node and the head
paragraphs: Node stores value and unique_ptr<Node> next. head owns the first node, and each next owns its successor. An empty head means an empty list. A valid model has neither ownership cycles nor a second owner of any node.
The ownership lesson introduced explicit Node(int v):value(v){} and ->. A raw Node* is only a traversal observer. It does not delete a node and must not outlive an update that destroys that node.

sections.title: Insertion at the front
paragraphs: Create a new unique_ptr, move head into newNode->next, then move newNode into head. Every node retains one owner at each step. unique_ptr copying is forbidden and must not be replaced with a copied raw address.
Pushing 1,2,3 at the front yields 3,2,1. That order follows from the operation, not a printing defect. To preserve input order, use a tail-insertion invariant or an appropriate standard container.

sections.title: Removal without losing ownership
paragraphs: To remove the head, first move head->next into a temporary next, then replace head with next. The old node is destroyed while the tail retains an owner. Check head first: -> through nullptr is invalid.

Do not use an observer of a removed node afterward. A before-and-after diagram is more useful than executing a dangling pointer. Removing an interior node requires the owning link; its value alone is insufficient when duplicates exist.

sections.title: Iterative cleanup
paragraphs: A unique_ptr chain may be destroyed recursively through next destructors. Huge lists can therefore have depth problems. This lesson bounds the count to 100 and also demonstrates iterative cleanup by detaching next before destroying the head.

while(head) detaches the tail into a temporary owner and replaces the head. Each step destroys exactly one node. Afterward head is empty and observers are no longer used. No shared_ptr or manual delete is required.

sections.title: Cost depends on the operation
paragraphs: Front insertion and head removal perform O(1) link changes. Searching by value is O(n). An O(1) removal claim assumes the required owning link is already known; locating that position may cost O(n).

vector stores elements compactly, while a list allocates nodes separately and stores links. vector is often simpler for an ordinary catalogue. The teaching list develops ownership reasoning; it is not automatically the right final-project container.

sections.title: Structural tests
paragraphs: Test empty, singleton, and three-node lists with duplicates, head removal, and complete cleanup. A live-node counter in the extra scaffold should return to zero. A value sum checks data but does not establish every link’s correctness.

Preserve traversal order, node counts, and before-and-after ownership diagrams. Next, stack and queue adapters provide LIFO or FIFO without manually linking nodes and combine queued commands with undo in the project.

assessment.question: What is the cost of finding an unknown value in a list?
assessment.explanation: Usually the chain must be traversed to reach the desired node.

assessment.question: What order results from pushFront(1), pushFront(2), pushFront(3)?
assessment.explanation: Each new node becomes the head.

assessment.question: Who releases a node in the unique_ptr model?
assessment.explanation: A raw Node* is used for observation.

assessment.question: Why demonstrate iterative cleanup?
answers: To avoid relying on a deep destructor chain
assessment.explanation: Detach next first, then destroy one node.

assessment.question: What is needed to accept this lab?
answers: Source, actual results, original tests, and a contract explanation
